subject: Tenant onboarding: epoxy-node IO slices, ephemeral cache fallback & retention tiers
messages:
From: Amanda Hart <amanda.hart@physicore.com>
To: diego_fernandez@redwood.com
Cc: ops-eng@physicore.com
Date: Tue, 15 Jun 2027 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Onboarding: IO slices, ephemeral cache fallback & retention tiers

Hi Diego,

Thanks again for the walkthrough this morning. We reviewed the preliminary sizing and have a couple of practical constraints I wanted to put on the table before the site workshop:

- We have two classes of storage available at our colo: hot NVMe (local, 1–2TB per host) and a shared NFS-backed slow tier (sized at 20TB).
- We will run three tenant profiles initially: production (low-latency), staging (bursty), and analytics (batch). Production must not be affected by noisy neighbors.
- Our compliance team requires 30d immutable retention on embeddings for audit, but short-lived caches for KV/replicas are fine.
- We are concerned about the behavior when local NVMe is full: will Redwood fall back to NFS (and what does that mean for latency/SLOs)?

Can you send a short runbook for: node selection (GPU vs cpu), how you recommend slicing node pools by io, expected eviction behavior, and an explicit fallback plan from NVMe -> NFS (including a rough cost/latency delta)? Also attaching our onboarding matrix (see: physicore_onboarding_matrix.xlsx) for environment specifics.

Appreciate a quick summary we can share with our infra team before Friday's site call.

Best,
Amanda
Amanda Hart
Head of Platform Ops
PhysiCore Medical

Date: Tue, 15 Jun 2027 10:03:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Onboarding: IO slices, ephemeral cache fallback & retention tiers

Amanda — thanks for the clear list. Quick summary up front: yes, Redwood supports an automatic NVMe -> remote-store fallback, but there are meaningful latency and token-cost implications; we recommend an explicit eviction + write-through policy instead of silent fallback for production tenants. Below is a concise plan and questions for Friday's workshop.

Plan outline (short):
1) Node roles & pools
   - prod-gpu (pinned to NVMe local; guaranteed QoS; taints + dedicated tenancy)
   - burst-cpu (staging; tolerate eviction; lower priority QoS)
   - analytics (batch; use NFS/slow tier; no local cache)

2) IO slicing and PV strategy
   - Local NVMe as ephemeral-provisioner for KV cache & runtime caches (emptyDir:memory-backed where possible), mounted with fsync optimizations.
   - Short-lived checkpoints (kv-snapshots) should be asynchronously written to NFS every 5–15 minutes for recovery.
   - Embeddings and audit logs -> persisted to encrypted NFS backed object store with 30d retention policy.

3) Fallback behavior (NVMe full or node loss)
   - Default: Pod eviction when local disk pressure hits soft threshold (80%), with graceful shutdown hooks to flush KV to NFS.
   - Prevent silent fallback for prod: mark prod tenants with nodeSelector and localPersistentVolume claims; if local capacity missing, traffic route falls back to a dedicated regional Redwood-hosted replica rather than NFS.

4) SLO/latency expectations
   - NVMe local: 5–15ms per token (depends on GPU batch).
   - NFS fallback: 80–200ms token delta; recommend limited read-only fallback for non-latency-sensitive features.

Open questions for PhysiCore team (please answer before Fri):
A) Do you want production to prefer cross-region Redwood-hosted replica rather than NFS fallback? (this implies egress/peering costs)
B) Are we allowed to install a small HA proxy in colo to tunnel KV flushes to your object store?
C) Expected size of in-memory KV cache per tenant (rough ballpark) — helps set eviction thresholds.

I'll attach a one-pager with the eviction thresholds and a sample DaemonSet to manage flush hooks before the call. Looping Neha for persistence and Monica for provisioning timelines.

— Diego
Diego Fernandez
Senior Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference
From: neha_kapoor@redwood.com <neha_kapoor@redwood.com>

Subject: Re: Onboarding: IO slices, ephemeral cache fallback & retention tiers

Adding a few technical guardrails from persistence side:

- PV classes: we should define three storageclasses in the cluster: local-nvme (non-reclaimable, local PV), shared-nfs-enc (NFS + at-rest encryption), and archive-object (S3-compatible for long-term embeddings).
- QoS and requests/limits: for prod-gpu nodepool, set storage.io.kubernetes.io/throughput to high, and reserve 30% of local NVMe for system/OS to avoid Kubernetes disk-pressure surprises.
- Flush cadence: implement a DaemonSet that watches for preStop and node pressure events and triggers a background rsync to NFS; attach a 60s deadline so requests are not hung indefinitely.
- Eviction policy: configure kubelet eviction thresholds: soft: nodefs.available < 15%, hard: < 5%. Soft triggers a graceful eviction with PodDisruptionBudget respect; hard will force kill.

Risk notes: if we allow silent fallback to NFS, embedding queries will see 2–3x latency and error amplification under load. For audit retention: use immutable buckets and object lifecycle rules; Redwood can tag objects with tenant metadata for easy purge/restore.

I've attached the cache IO sim results we ran against your sample workload — helps size NVMe per-prod-tenant.

— Neha
Neha Kapoor
Principal SRE, Redwood Inference
